text:
Interviewer: This is a United States Holocaust Memorial Museum volunteer collection interview with Pete Miller, conducted by Jack Smith, on March 6, 2007, in Silver Spring, Maryland. This is tape number one, side A. What is your full name?
Interviewee: Pete Miller.
Interviewer: That is the name you were born with?
Interviewee: No. In Poland I called Pietey Miller.
Interviewer: Did you have a middle name?
Interviewee: A middle? No.
Interviewer: And where were you born and when were you born?
Interviewee: I was born in Poland, the city name’s Łoch w, December 7, 1925.
Interviewer: And that is n-near what large city?
Interviewee: Near Kalisz, Sieradz, Wieluń, little larger cities.
Interviewer: Mm-hm, mm-hm. And I understand it’s 69 kilometers southwest of L dz?
Interviewee: Yeah, something like that, yes, mm-hm.
Interviewer: Let’s talk about your family. How long had your father’s — well, t-tell me about your father’s family.
Interviewee: My father, well, he had the family too, but they were far away from us. My mother had a lot of families, brothers, and they’re all married and have a lot of children too. But they’re all, they’re all grown, you know.
Interviewer: What was your father’s name?
Interviewee: My father’s name was Hans Ernst.
Interviewer: And where was he born?
Interviewee: He was born in Łoch w, too, yes.
Interviewer: Did he had a large extended family, brothers and sisters?
Interviewee: Not a lot, but he have some, yes.
Interviewer: And what kind of work did your father do?
Interviewee: He was a furrier, not to make coats, but th-th-the fur came da — came off on the — from the animals, he stretched it and dried it and sold it to — to the — to the ti — tailors, and the one who made those coats.
Interviewer: And your mother’s name?
Interviewee: Morgan.
Interviewer: And her maiden name?
Interviewee: Cox.
Interviewer: And what — tell me about her family.
Interviewee: Her family, she had brothers, and they all married, they have a lot of chi — *** children, I say one of them have about seven, seven children, all girls. They live in Poland, another one lived in — in Belgium. *** also married, but he had children, I don’t know how many he had. They both a large family, yes.
Interviewer: And did you have any brothers or sisters?
Interviewee: I had one brother, older brother. Older brother.
Interviewer: And what is his name?
Interviewee: His name is Elisa. Elisa.
Interviewer: Okay. And where — can you describe the town to me, and the neighborhood that you lived in when you were a small child?
Interviewee: It was a small town, and the Jew wasn’t welcome very much there, the anti-Semitism was great. You went to show, they throw at you rocks, you know, then it wa — it was very, very unpleasant, the last years in Poland.
Interviewer: Well, but let’s talk about the earlier years, your earlier childhood. What kind of neighborhood did you live in? Was it a Jewish neighborhood, or wa —
Interviewee: It was mixed. It was a mixed neighborhood, Jewish and — and — and Poles.
Interviewer: And did you have non-Jewish friends as a young child?
Interviewee: We have some who went to public school. We’d be *** together. Then I went to cheder, to the Jewish school, you know, I learn Hebrew and Yiddish, writing, reading.
Interviewer: So, was your family religious? It sounded like they wanted you to have a good religious education.
Interviewee: They were religious, yes. No — not — not really ha-ha-Hasidim, no, but they were religious, went to shul, and we did what is supposed — a Jew is supposed to do, sure.
Interviewer: And what languages did you speak?
Interviewee: We speak Yiddish all the time, even now with my wife, we speak only Yiddish home. Only we go out to buy things, then we talk English.
Interviewer: But when you were growing up you spoke Yiddish to your brother and to your parents?
Interviewee: Yes, Yiddish only.
Interviewer: Yeah. And what about in school?
Interviewee: In public school, at the — at — with the — on-only Polish, of course. But I went to cheder, that was Yiddish, and reading and writing, we did all that.
Interviewer: Did you have any favorite holidays as a young child?
Interviewee: Every holiday was a good holiday when you don’t have to go to school.
Interviewer: Can you describe one of the hol — the holidays that you remember?
Interviewee: Na — Purim was nice. Hanukkah was nice, we — you get gifts, that was always nice.
Interviewer: Did y — a-and you had mentioned something about anti-Semitic experiences you had. Any other ones that you can talk about — when you — this was when you were a child, when you were a child.
Interviewee: I don’t know what you mean by that.
Interviewer: Any other ti — kinds of anti-Semitic incidents that you remember when you were a child? Anything that people said or did.
Interviewee: The Poles didn’t like the Jews. Tha-That’s for sure, they didn’t like us.
Interviewer: How did you know that, as a child?
Interviewee: Because they — they — they throw rocks as they went to shul, they spit on us and all kind of things. And th-they had the expression they use. And what does that mean? The Jews to Palestine, then.
Interviewer: And did you talk this over with your parents?
Interviewee: Well, they know it. Th-They knew — th-they knew better than I did. Sure.
Interviewer: Did they say anything special to comfort you as a young boy?
Interviewee: Not really. We didn’t talk too much about it, we have to be careful. If you see them, don’t — avoid them, you know. Avoid them. Don’t — do-don’t face them. Something like that.
Interviewer: Were your parents Zionists?
Interviewee: Yes, they were Zionists, yes.
Interviewer: Did they belong to any organizations, and if so, which ones?
Interviewee: Can’t recall now, ut — but it — they were — I was young then. No, I don’t recall that, where — where they belonged or not.
Interviewer: And tell me about your brother. Were you close to your brother while you both were young?
Interviewee: Yes. He was a little bit older. We were close, sure, absolutely.
Interviewer: And did you do — what — what kind of sports — were you interested in sports?
Interviewee: Well, like kids we just kicked the ball. I was young, there was nothing — nothing else. Not any particular sport, no.
Interviewer: Tell me, did your family and you do any traveling before conditions got bad?
Interviewee: No, not too much, I don’t recall that, no. We only went to our uncle, it wasn’t too far, on the holiday or so, and that’s about it.
Interviewer: And what kind of activities did you do in your free time? What — did you have any hobbies?
Interviewee: Just lay around with the — with the friends I had, and that’s all. Nothing special.
Interviewer: Would — would you describe your family as middle class? Ho-How would you describe them, economically?
Interviewee: Middle class, yes.
Interviewer: And tell me about your home. Was it an apartment or a house?
Interviewee: A house, it was a house, yes.
Interviewer: Can you describe it to me?
Interviewee: It was a small house, enough for us. We were comfortable living in it. That was nice.
Interviewer: Did you and your brother have your own bedrooms?
Interviewee: Yes, yes.
Interviewer: Tell me about your Bar Mitzvah.
Interviewee: The Bar Mitzvah, yes, I went to — went to shul, had my Bar Mitzvah. You know, have a — all the goodies after, you know, and it w — it was nice, very nice. I enjoyed it.
Interviewer: Now — well now, let’s start talking about when conditions started to change. You said you were born in 1925, so when were you aware that problems were beginning?
Interviewee: Oh, soon after the Germans — the Germany occupied Poland, beginning in 1940 —
Interviewer: O-Okay, so up to that time, up to that time, had you heard of a man named Hitler, who came into power in 1933? As a child, did you hear anything about him?
Interviewee: We heard about Hitler, yes.
Interviewer: And what did your parents say about him?
Interviewee: They couldn’t say very well, maybe it — maybe it going to be all right, maybe he’ll — he’ll die or something, something like that, but nothing we can do. We were — we — we born there and we made the living there, and we can’t run just like that.
Interviewer: Was your mother working?
Interviewee: No, she was home now, homemaker.
Interviewer: So up to 1939, when the war started, you just had a regular childhood, and playing with friends and so forth?
Interviewee: Regular childhood, yes, playing with friends. It was nice, yes.
Interviewer: All right, and then comes September 1939, what are your first memories of that, when the Germans invaded Poland?
Interviewee: ’39 wasn’t too bad yet, but beginning of — of 1940, they gather all the Jews, you know, and they kicked the Poles out and they give them better homes, where the Jews were living, and they created what you call a ghetto. And that was it. Lived all — all the Jews there in the ghetto.
